title: From Abu Dhabi to Amsterdam: Inside Modi's Five-Nation Sprint to Secure India's Energy and Trade Future
excerpt: The Prime Minister's six-day tour across the UAE, Netherlands, Sweden, Norway and Italy is less a diplomatic courtesy call than a high-stakes bid to lock in LPG supplies, semiconductor partnerships and a $70 billion trade corridor.
body:
When Prime Minister Narendra Modi stepped off his aircraft in Abu Dhabi on May 15 to the roar of an F-16 escort and a guard of honour from the UAE Presidential Guard, the optics were unmistakable. India was not visiting — it was arriving.

## The stakes in the Gulf

The UAE stop anchors a five-nation tour that spans the Gulf and northern Europe, and it is the most consequential of the lot. India and the UAE signed fresh memoranda of understanding on liquefied petroleum gas cooperation and strategic petroleum reserves, a direct response to the energy anxiety triggered by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. With oil prices elevated and shipping insurance costs through the roof, the agreement to secure long-term LPG supplies from Abu Dhabi's state-owned ADNOC is intended to cushion Indian households from further price shocks.

Bilateral trade between the two countries has already touched $100 billion, and both governments now aim to double that figure by 2032. The Indian diaspora in the UAE — 4.5 million strong, the largest expatriate community in the Gulf — watched the arrival with particular interest. Many had lobbied for relief measures on remittance costs and consular backlogs; the visit has reportedly produced a framework for reduced transfer fees through India's UPI-to-NEFT bridge.

## A semiconductor courtship in Europe

From Abu Dhabi, Modi heads to the Netherlands, where the agenda shifts sharply from hydrocarbons to high technology. The Dutch leg is squarely about semiconductors. India has courted ASML, the only company on earth that manufactures extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, for the better part of two years. While a manufacturing deal remains elusive, a bilateral "semiconductor corridor" agreement is expected that would smooth technology licensing and supply-chain integration for India's nascent chip fabs in Gujarat and Assam.

The Netherlands visit also carries quieter diplomatic significance. The Dutch government recently repatriated 1,000-year-old Chola-era copper plates to India after a 14-year diplomatic campaign — a gesture that New Delhi acknowledged warmly in pre-trip readouts.

## Nordic energy and defence bets

Sweden and Norway round out the European itinerary with discussions on green hydrogen, offshore wind, and defence partnerships. India's interest in Scandinavian clean-energy technology has grown sharply as New Delhi races to meet its 500-gigawatt renewable target by 2030. Norwegian sovereign wealth fund officials have signalled willingness to expand their already sizable Indian equity holdings, subject to governance improvements.

For the Federation of Indian Export Organisations, the tour has material implications: FIEO estimates the five bilateral tracks could unlock $70 billion in new trade flows, concentrated in engineering goods, green energy equipment, and digital services.

## What it means for the diaspora

For NRIs, the significance stretches beyond geopolitics. The tour addresses three longstanding pain points. First, energy security: a disruption to Gulf supply chains would hit remittance-earning households on both sides. Second, semiconductor supply: Indian tech professionals in the Netherlands and across Europe are increasingly caught between export-control regimes and their employers' India operations. Third, cultural restitution: the return of heritage artefacts from European museums has become a matter of identity for diaspora communities who have funded temple restorations and cultural endowments for decades.

Modi's final stop is Rome, where discussions on the India-EU free trade agreement — stalled since 2013 — could gain new momentum. A deal, if struck, would affect everything from Indian pharmaceutical exports to European agricultural standards.

The tour ends on May 20. By then, India's diplomatic calendar will already be crowded with the G20 finance ministers' meeting and World Cup 2026 preparations. But for a few days, at least, the message from New Delhi is simple: India is negotiating on multiple fronts, with multiple partners, and it intends to close.
